strengths: Novel algorithmic contributions: LLPF_M2M and LLPF_M2O algorithms are well-designed with clever use of variance sphere geometry and variance correction mechanisms

Extensive experimental validation across multiple architectures (LeNet5, ResNet18, CCT7, MobileNet, ShuffleNet) and datasets (MNIST, CIFAR10, CIFAR100, ImageNet1k) with consistent results across 10-200 repetitions
Excellent reproducibility: comprehensive hyperparameter tables, detailed algorithms, appendices with equation validations, and computational cost transparency
Practical improvements demonstrated: +0.79% accuracy gain on ImageNet1k (69.758% to 70.55%) without additional augmentation
Multiple complementary analyses: PCA visualization, dimensionality analysis via SVD, generalization-distance relationships provide multi-faceted investigation
Narrow standard deviation bands across repetitions demonstrate algorithm consistency and reliability
weaknesses: Central claim about 'fully connected' space is overstated: the requirement for layer-by-layer sequential processing in manually determined order (Table 1) contradicts the connectivity claim and is insufficiently highlighted in main text

Critical train-test loss gap undermines practical significance: Figure 2 clearly shows that low training loss does NOT guarantee low test loss, especially for ResNet18; the acknowledged solution is to operate 'within training-defined low-loss space' which limits utility

Limited theoretical novelty: core findings (continuous low-loss regions) directly derive from Watanabe's Singular Learning Theory (1993-2018) and prior empirical work (Garipov et al. 2018, Draxler et al. 2018); the contribution is primarily algorithmic rather than conceptual

Restrictive prerequisites substantially limit generality: requires flat minima (not sharp), nearby variance spheres (not universal), and architecture-specific hyperparameter tuning with no principled selection method

Key approximations lack sufficient justification: Equation 5 (Mean≈0) has non-negligible deviations (Figure 7: some layers show mean ~10^-1); Equation 6's proportionality derivation doesn't address constant n; VarianceCorrection target value v appears circular

Dimensionality analysis lacks statistical rigor: SVD-based claim 'all parameters matter' specifies neither the number of paths constructed nor provides statistical tests; result states equality to 'minimum of paths or dimensionality' which is trivially true
High computational expense severely limits reproducibility and adoption: ResNet18/CIFAR10 requires 24 hours on H100; ImageNet1k requires 340 hours with no analysis of cost reduction

Incomplete comparison with AutoNEB: claims of 'lower maximum loss' shown for only one configuration; fails to discuss AutoNEB's advantages; 'consistency' measured only on training metrics not test loss
Layer ordering for complex models appears empirically determined without principled methodology: how should practitioners apply this to new architectures?

Limited experiments on generalization models: Appendix A.4 admits additional architecture experiments (MobileNet, ShuffleNet) 'repeated only once' due to computational constraints, undermining reproducibility claims for those results

strengths: Well-motivated research question on loss landscape geometry and connectivity of low-loss regions
Extensive experimental validation across multiple architectures (LeNet5, ResNet18, CCT7, MobileNet, ShuffleNet) and datasets with repeated runs for statistical consistency
Clear algorithmic exposition with geometric intuitions, detailed derivations, and comprehensive hyperparameter documentation
Honest discussion of limitations, prerequisites, and failure cases (e.g., flat minima requirement, VGG16 failure)
Practical demonstration on ImageNet1k showing potential utility for improving generalization
weaknesses: Core finding that low-loss regions are connected is not novel—already established by AutoNEB (Draxler et al. 2018) and Garipov et al. (2018), making this work incremental rather than fundamentally new
Variance sphere framework lacks theoretical justification; the choice of variance as the constraining quantity appears ad-hoc and is validated only empirically, not derived from first principles

Algorithm requires extensive manual hyperparameter tuning with layer-specific configuration (8 phases for ResNet18/CCT7), severely limiting generalizability and practical applicability across architectures

Restrictive prerequisites (flat minima, nearby variance spheres per Eq. 4) are only empirically validated for ResNet18 and not universally applicable; algorithm fails for some architectures (VGG16 without batch norm)

Overclaimed 'no parameter redundancy' finding: SVD results show full-dimensionality of low-loss space but do not imply individual parameters are non-redundant; conflates space-level properties with point-level properties

Generalization improvements are modest and improperly evaluated: Algorithm 2's finding that closer-to-origin models generalize better restates well-known regularization theory; no ablation comparing against standard L2/weight decay; ImageNet improvement (~0.8%) lacks statistical significance testing

Core theoretical claims lack rigor: 'continuous and fully connected' are informal rather than formally proven; no convergence analysis, no characterization of when variance constraints enable path-finding, no theorems provided
PCA visualizations (Figures 4, 9) provide limited insight; interpretations are speculative without rigorous evidence; claimed 'layer-wise diagnostic tool' is unsubstantiated
Weak comparison with prior work: AutoNEB comparison is indirect using different architectures/datasets; some experiments run only once due to computational constraints (Figure 8)

Missing critical experiments: no statistical significance testing on improvements, no ablation studies on algorithm components (e.g., variance correction step), no sensitivity analysis for hyperparameters

strengths: Well-motivated research question addressing fundamental aspects of neural network loss landscape geometry
Clear mathematical formalization of low-loss space with rigorous definitions (Equation 1) and elegant variance sphere framework
Novel algorithmic contributions (LLPF_M2M and LLPF_M2O) with detailed pseudocode and geometric intuition
Extensive experimental validation across multiple architectures (LeNet5, ResNet18, CCT7) with 200, 40, and 10 repetitions respectively
Thorough empirical validation of key assumptions in appendices (Equations 3-6) demonstrating methodological rigor
Excellent reproducibility: comprehensive hyperparameter tables (Tables 1-5), computation times, detailed preprocessing steps, and multiple validation metrics
Interesting geometric insights including finding that low-loss space spans full parameter dimensionality, challenging conventional over-parameterization views
Novel PCA-based visualization revealing layer-wise feature properties and landscape sharpness characteristics

weaknesses: Algorithm 1 requires careful layer-by-layer manual tuning with architecture-specific ordering (6-8 phases for ResNet18, Table 1), undermining claims of general applicability and raising reproducibility concerns
Critical prerequisite that models lie on nearby variance spheres (Equation 4) only empirically validated for ResNet18@CIFAR10; not universal and limits algorithm applicability
Algorithm fails with certain optimizers (Adam) for ResNet18, converging to sharp minima—suggests brittleness to training conditions rather than fundamental robustness

Limited theoretical justification: connection to Singular Learning Theory mentioned but not developed; lacks rigorous explanation for why low-loss space should be fully connected

Experimental scope limited to vision domain (MNIST, CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet1k) with only small-scale models (8-layer CCT7); scalability to modern large transformers unclear
Modest practical improvements (0.8% on ImageNet1k) achieved only after extensive architecture-specific hyperparameter tuning; computational cost (48 hours for CCT7) limits practical accessibility
Key prerequisites ('flat' low-loss regions, variance sphere membership) are difficult to verify a priori, creating chicken-and-egg problem for algorithm application
Approximations (Equations 5-6) insufficiently justified: Equation 5 validation (Appendix A.2) shows only order-of-magnitude consistency, not precise verification
Limited engagement with prior mode connectivity work (Garipov et al., Draxler et al.); AutoNEB comparison somewhat unfair given different objectives (test vs. training loss)

strengths: Extends mode connectivity to modern architectures (MobileNet, ShuffleNet, EfficientNet, RegNet, DLA, CCT), addressing a real gap in prior work limited to older CNNs and ResNets
Demonstrates strong reproducibility with consistent results across 10+ random seeds, a significant improvement over inconsistent prior methods (AutoNEB, FGE, SPRO)
Novel evaluation setting: connects modes trained with different hyperparameters (e.g., different weight decay), going beyond prior work restricted to identical training configurations
Comprehensive experimental validation with detailed metrics (training loss, test loss, accuracy, L2 distances), continuity checks, and extensive hyperparameter documentation enabling reproducibility
Geometric framework (variance spheres) provides useful intuition, with empirical validation of key mathematical relationships in appendices
weaknesses: Critical limitation: no guarantee of test loss/accuracy along discovered paths; paper shows test loss increases despite low training loss (Figure 2, ResNet18), severely limiting practical utility since generalization is the real concern

Requires manual specification of layer ordering; while FDF strategy proposed, complex models need 21+ sequentially ordered phases (Table 2), contradicting claims of generality and requiring significant architecture-specific engineering

Limited theoretical novelty: primarily applies existing layer-wise mode connectivity concepts (Adilova et al., 2024) to additional architectures without advancing theoretical understanding of why/when mode connectivity exists

Vague prerequisite conditions: 'flat minima' requirement lacks rigorous definition; only stated that 'near-zero training loss are generally flat' with no algorithmic verification method or systematic analysis of when assumption fails

No direct head-to-head comparison with prior methods on modern architectures; Table 1 uses reported numbers from different papers with different experimental setups, making relative improvements unclear
High computational cost (21-45 GPU hours, Table 6) without clear practical applications beyond theoretical landscape understanding; unclear when LLPF should be preferred over simpler alternatives

Lacks systematic analysis of generalization gap: paper identifies that test loss diverges from training loss but provides no investigation of causes, inherent limitations, or potential solutions beyond listing as a limitation
Algorithm 2 exhibits concerning asymmetry: only works toward origin due to exploding gradients in reverse direction; limited analysis of why this fundamental constraint exists

Insufficient hyperparameter sensitivity analysis despite introducing numerous hyperparameters (step_a, step_c, step_f, r, T); claims that 'only layer selection and order determine success' are not empirically validated through ablations
Missing ablation studies on key components (variance correction step, angle conformal step) and limited analysis of why certain layer orderings work better than others

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8+ modern architectures (MobileNet, EfficientNet, RegNet, DLA, CCT) on multiple datasets—extending mode connectivity beyond classical architectures where prior work focused
Demonstrates reproducible training loss trajectories across independent mode pairs trained with different random seeds, achieving consistent path discovery (~10+ repetitions per experiment)
Extends mode connectivity to modes trained with different hyperparameters (e.g., different weight decay values), a novel setting not evaluated by prior work
Transparent about fundamental limitations: clearly acknowledges in Section 6 that test accuracy is not preserved along discovered paths
Extensive implementation documentation (hyperparameter tables, detailed appendix with 21+ phases for complex architectures) supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Critical generalization failure: test accuracy degrades significantly along discovered paths despite low training loss (Figure 2: ResNet18 test loss increases from ~0.48 to ~0.62). Without test performance guarantees, practical utility is unclear and motivation contradicts prior work (AutoNEB/FGE) aimed at preserving generalization
Prohibitive computational cost (21-45 hours on H100/RTX-5090 per path, Table 6) makes the method impractical—training new models from scratch is likely faster, undercutting any value proposition

Method requires extensive architecture-specific hyperparameter engineering (DLA requires 21 sequential phases, CCT7 requires 9 phases with hand-tuned layer specifications). Claims 'only layer selection and order determine success' contradicts the substantial tuning required, limiting generalizability to new architectures

Weak theoretical foundations: Equation 5 (Mean≈0) is violated with means up to 3×10⁻¹ (Figure 8); Equations 4 and 6 rely on loose approximations without sensitivity analysis; the role of variance spheres in enabling mode connectivity is not mechanistically justified

Reproducibility claim is misleading: reported as 'consistent training loss trajectories' but test accuracy varies substantially (standard deviations visible in Figures 2-3); reproducibility across seeds ≠ algorithm stability

No controlled experimental comparisons: Table 1 compares against different methods on different models from different papers, not head-to-head. Lacks ablation studies on variance correction and angle conformal steps

Limited novelty: primarily applies layer-wise connectivity from Adilova et al. (2024) to additional architectures. Variance correction and angle conformal steps are straightforward engineering without fundamental algorithmic innovation
Vague prerequisites: 'flat low-loss regions' requirement (p. 7) is ill-defined. How is flatness measured? How to ensure models satisfy this condition in practice?

No demonstrated downstream applications: without test accuracy preservation and despite computational expense, no applications justify these paths (e.g., improved ensembles, model understanding, training acceleration)

Limited experimental scope: only CIFAR-10/100 and MNIST. No ImageNet or large-scale validation. No sensitivity analysis for step_a, step_c, step_f hyperparameters. Continuity check (Figure 5) only validates local linear interpolation, not entire path

strengths: Addresses a clear practical gap by extending mode connectivity to modern architectures (MobileNet, EfficientNet, RegNet, ShuffleNet, DLA, CCT), whereas prior methods were limited to older designs like LeNet, VGG, and ResNet

Comprehensive empirical validation with consistent results: experiments repeated ≥10 times per setting, detailed hyperparameter documentation (Tables 2-5), and validation of theoretical assumptions in appendix
Reproducibility improvements: high consistency across random seeds is a genuine advance over AutoNEB/FGE, with hundreds of validation simulations
Novel contribution of connecting modes on different variance spheres, extending beyond identical training hyperparameters—not evaluated in prior work
Clear and well-organized presentation with effective geometric illustrations (especially Figure 1) and formal mathematical definitions of key concepts
Strong experimental design with continuity validation (Figure 5) supporting path feasibility and extensive supplementary results across multiple datasets
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: the core insight of using layer-wise connectivity builds directly on Adilova et al. (2024); this is primarily an engineering contribution applying existing theory to new contexts rather than introducing fundamental new understanding

Critical limitation on test loss: the algorithm provides no guarantees for low test loss along paths (ResNet18 in Figure 2 shows increasing test loss), significantly limiting applicability for ensemble improvement or knowledge transfer—this fundamental gap undermines key motivating use cases
Substantial computational cost (45 hours for DLA@CIFAR10, 24 hours for CCT7) limits reproducibility and practical adoption, especially for resource-constrained researchers

Architecture-specific manual tuning required: despite the FDF strategy, layer ordering still demands manual determination for many models; paper explicitly states 'layer orders are determined manually' for non-FDF cases, reducing generality and ease of use

Strong assumptions with limited theoretical justification: Equation 5 (Mean ≈ 0) and Equation 4 (variance preservation) are empirically validated but approximation error impacts are not characterized; no sensitivity analysis provided
Limited experimental scope: all experiments use small-scale models on CIFAR/MNIST; no ImageNet-scale validation or evaluation on very deep architectures, leaving scalability questions unresolved
Missing hyperparameter sensitivity analysis: no systematic study of sensitivity to step_a, step_c, step_f; Figure 6 shows tuning improves results but principled guidance is absent
Incomplete failure mode analysis: limited discussion beyond sharp minima of when/why LLPF fails; no method provided for verifying the 'flat low-loss region' prerequisite a priori
Algorithm 2 asymmetry underexplored: the reverse direction (toward larger variance spheres) fails due to exploding gradients, suggesting incomplete geometric intuition
Table 1 comparisons limited: notes worst-case losses are 'not strictly comparable across papers due to differing models'; more controlled comparisons would strengthen claims

strengths: Comprehensive experimental validation across diverse architectures (ResNet, DLA, CCT, EfficientNet, MobileNet, etc.) and datasets with hundreds of trials demonstrating reproducibility
Meaningful practical improvement: LLPF achieves consistent paths across random seeds while AutoNEB shows high variability (0.5-1.5 range), advancing the reliability of mode connectivity methods
Clear technical presentation with good geometric intuition; well-structured algorithms with thorough ablations (Appendix I) validating each component
First demonstration of mode connectivity in modern architectures (transformers, efficient nets) extending beyond traditional CNNs, addressing open question from introduction
Novel contribution: supports connecting modes trained with different hyperparameters (different variance spheres), a setting not evaluated by prior work
Honest discussion of limitations: acknowledges test loss degradation, hyperparameter sensitivity, and theoretical gaps rather than overclaiming
Rigorous comparison with prior work: identifies bug in FGE's released code and provides fair assessment against AutoNEB with detailed analysis
weaknesses: Limited theoretical foundation: Equations 4-5 (variance preservation, zero mean) empirically validated but lack theoretical justification for why these properties hold; no convergence guarantees for algorithms; approximation errors not bounded

Substantial hyperparameter complexity contradicts claims of simplicity: despite stating 'only layer selection determines success,' Tables 4-5 show extensive architecture-specific tuning (step_f, step_a, step_c, T, r); heuristic FDF layer-ordering strategy lacks principled justification; no systematic guidance for new architectures

Critical test loss limitation: Algorithm 1 does not guarantee low testing loss; Figure 2 shows test loss increasing despite low training loss, suggesting paths occupy training-defined regions without generalization; fundamental gap between training and test performance largely unexamined

Prohibitive computational cost: ResNet18@CIFAR10 requires ~21 hours on H100; CCT7 requires ~25 hours on RTX 3090; no complexity analysis; makes reproducibility claims less meaningful if paths take days to compute; scalability to full ImageNet and modern large models unclear

Limited conceptual novelty: builds heavily on Adilova et al. (2024) layer-wise connectivity; main contribution is engineering a practical algorithm rather than new insights; sequential layer processing approach is heuristic without theoretical analysis of why it succeeds

Narrow evaluation scope: limited to small-scale image classification (CIFAR-10/100, MNIST); ImageNet10 is artificial 10-class subset; uses ResNet18/small transformers; no evaluation on other domains (NLP, RL); generalization of findings questionable

Incomplete hyperparameter reproducibility: code availability mentioned but no link provided; Table 4 hyperparameters are extensive; practitioners cannot easily apply LLPF to new settings without reverse-engineering or trial-and-error

Missing theoretical analysis: approximation in Equation 5 shows non-negligible deviations (±0.01 range) in Appendix B; error propagation through sequential layer updates not analyzed; why layer-wise processing solves linear interpolation failure unexplored

strengths: Demonstrates mode connectivity across modern architectures (MobileNet, EfficientNet, CCT, DLA, RegNet) beyond prior work
Shows reproducibility with consistent path properties across hundreds of random seeds, absent from AutoNEB/FGE
First work evaluating cross-hyperparameter connectivity (different variance spheres)
Extensive empirical validation with comprehensive ablations and hyperparameter documentation
Clear geometric intuition and well-organized presentation with informative appendices
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core insight (layer-wise connectivity) is from Adilova et al. 2024; paper applies existing framework rather than introducing new ideas

Unfair baseline comparisons: Table 9 compares AutoNEB (ResNet20) vs LLPF (ResNet18); FGE comparison problematic since prior work had bugs rather than inherent limitations; no comparison with recent mode connectivity work
Extremely high computational cost: 21-45 GPU-hours per connection vs ~3 hours for training (7-15× multiplier); cost justification not discussed
